title: XSS, CSRF, injection and tokens
subtitle: Every input is hostile until proven otherwise. See how the classic attacks work — and the one habit that stops each.

sections.title: The security mindset
sections.body: Never trust client input; give the least privilege; layer defences; fail closed. The OWASP Top 10 lists the most common flaws (broken access control, injection, cryptographic failures, insecure design, …). HTTPS protects data in transit but does nothing about these bugs.

questions.prompt: Validation in the browser alone is…

choices.text: Not enough: an attacker can skip the browser.

sections.title: SQL injection
sections.body: Pasting input into SQL: "SELECT * FROM users WHERE name='" + n + "'" with n = ' OR '1'='1 returns every user. Fix: parameterised queries (WHERE name = ?) so the input is always data, never code.

questions.prompt: The standard defence against SQL injection is…

figures.caption: Figure 5.2.1 — SQL injection
figures.note: The quote in the input closes the string.

sections.title: Cross-site scripting (XSS)
sections.body: If a site echoes user text into a page unescaped, an attacker can make it include <script> that runs in victims’ browsers with the site’s privileges (stealing cookies, acting as them). Defences: escape output for its context, a Content-Security-Policy, HttpOnly cookies, and frameworks that escape by default.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: < becomes < so it cannot start a tag.

figures.note: Stored XSS hits everyone who views the comment.

sections.title: Cross-site request forgery (CSRF)
sections.body: While you are logged in to a bank, a malicious page makes your browser send POST /transfer — the browser attaches your cookie automatically. Defences: a secret CSRF token in forms, SameSite cookies, re-authenticating for sensitive actions.

choices.text: The attacker’s page cannot read or guess it.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: The server checks the token matches.

figures.caption: Figure 5.4.1 — CSRF
figures.note: The bank cannot tell the request was not intended.

sections.title: Passwords and tokens
sections.body: Never store passwords in plain text: store a salted, slow hash (bcrypt, scrypt, Argon2). The salt is random per user, so identical passwords hash differently and rainbow tables fail; slowness limits guessing. Add rate limiting and multi-factor authentication. A password of length L over an alphabet of A symbols has AL possibilities.

worked.why: Number of passwords ≈ 2.1 × 10¹¹; with A = 94 printable symbols it is 94⁸ ≈ 6.1 × 10¹⁵, about 29 000× more.

choices.text: Precomputed (rainbow table) attacks and duplicate hashes.

sections.title: Security headers and a checklist
sections.body:
• HTTPS everywhere with HSTS
  • Content-Security-Policy
  • Escape output, parameterise queries
  • Hash passwords with salt
  • CSRF tokens + SameSite cookies
  • Least privilege; update dependencies

questions.prompt: Which measure reduces the damage of an XSS bug?

choices.text: A strict Content-Security-Policy and HttpOnly cookies.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Limits what injected script can do.
